@fig-ignitions shows the same records season by season, and the fall of both completeness measures after 2000 made the cause split unreadable as an ignition trend. Three response series were therefore modelled, lightning, person-caused and all causes together, because the all-cause series was unaffected by cause coding and so decided any disagreement. Detection of small fires also improved over the record, so every result was reported at three minimum fire sizes, no limit, one hectare and four hectares, and a conclusion that survived at only one was reported as not surviving.

## Study Design

FWI1987 and FWI2025 differed at once in model version and in the time resolution of the weather, so a direct comparison could attribute a difference to neither. Three series were therefore computed from the one hourly weather record, so that each contrast between two of them changed one thing (@tbl-design).

| Series | System  | Weather input               | Pathway                        |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| S1     | FWI1987 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | the legacy configuration       |
| S2     | FWI2025 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | pathway C of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |
| S3     | FWI2025 | observed hourly weather     | pathway A of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |

: The three fire danger series and what separates them. {#tbl-design}

The contrast of S1 against S2 isolated the version change at a fixed input, and S2 against S3 the change of input resolution at a fixed version. S1 against S3 was the change an agency met in moving from the old system to the new. All three ran on the same weather, season window, startup values and gap filling, so no difference came from the record itself.

Under pathway C the 13:00 observation was converted to estimated daily maxima and minima with the report's national constants. Those extremes were expanded to an hourly stream by the sinusoidal method of @beck1989diurnal, with the default offset and decay coefficients of Table A-1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025 and rainfall at the first hour after sunrise.

## Index Computation

FWI2025 was computed with the reference implementation of the Canadian Forest Service Fire Danger Group [@nrcan2026cffdrsng], run unmodified, which reproduced its distributed standard output exactly over the 2,623 hour test record from the Petawawa Research Forest. FWI1987 was implemented for this study in Python and checked in two ways reported in Appendix A, against the `cffdrs` package, version 1.9.2 [@wang2017cffdrs; @wang2026cffdrspkg], and against the codes that BC Wildfire Service computed operationally at these stations.

Where the System as printed in @vanwagner1987fwi differed from the Fortran listing of @vanwagner1985fortran, the implementation followed the listing, taking the exact coefficient 147.2772 that converted the Fine Fuel Moisture Code to a moisture content rather than the rounded 147.2.

## Seasonal Metrics

For each station-season and series, twelve seasonal metrics were computed over the window. Six were levels, the mean Fire Weather Index, the seasonal severity rating, the sum of the Daily Severity Rating over the season, the peak Buildup Index, the mean Initial Spread Index, the mean Duff Moisture Code and the peak Drought Code, and six were counts of days at or above the thresholds described next. The FWI2025 series were summarised to a daily value at 16:00 Local Standard Time, the conventional peak burn hour, with the daily maximum kept as a sensitivity only.

Absolute thresholds applied unchanged to all three series. A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 was taken from section 4.1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025 so that days at or above it tested that report's comparability sentence, and was the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System's extreme class for the code [@field2015gfwed]. A Fire Weather Index of 30 was that system's extreme class [@field2015gfwed], and a Fire Weather Index of 19 was the fire spread day threshold of @podur2011spread.

Relative thresholds followed @zhang2011indices, the 90th and 95th percentiles of each series' own Fire Weather Index distribution, and the 95th percentile of its Initial Spread Index distribution, the fire weather day threshold of @richardson2022global applied to the spread index, at each station over the 1991 to 2020 reference period, the current World Meteorological Organization normal. Inside that period the mean count above the 90th percentile was near ten per cent of days in every series by construction, so only the trend of a relative count said anything about the version.

Counts above the relative thresholds in base-period seasons were estimated by the bootstrap of @zhang2005percentile, adapted from a daily to a seasonal threshold. For each base season the threshold was re-estimated with that season removed and each other base season duplicated in turn in its place, and the count was the mean over those replacements. The last `r yr_last - 2020` seasons used the threshold from the whole base period.

## Statistical Analysis

Trends were estimated with the Theil-Sen slope [@sen1968slope] and tested with the Mann-Kendall test [@mann1945nonparametric] over the `r n_seasons` kept seasons from `r yr_first` to `r yr_last`, on the actual season years so that a gap was kept as a gap.

Significance was assessed under the variance correction of @hamed1998mmk for serial correlation, without which the test rejected too often on trendless series [@yue2002autocorrelation; @bayazit2007prewhiten]. Because the correction counted lags in observations rather than years, across a gap left by the coverage rule it was understated, so a marginal q value, the p value after correction for multiple testing, was weaker than it read.

Within each station's twelve metrics in each series, p values were corrected by the false discovery rate procedure of @benjamini1995fdr, which @benjamini2001dependency proved still controlled that rate under positive regression dependency, the case here. The confidence interval on a slope was the percentile interval over 2,000 moving-block bootstrap resamples of seasons.

The difference between two series' slopes was tested on the differences themselves, following @santer2000trenddiff, by a moving-block bootstrap, because the three series were mutually dependent and serially correlated [@kunsch1989bootstrap; @politis1994stationary]. Each of the 4,000 replicates drew blocks of consecutive seasons with replacement and recomputed both slopes on the same resampled seasons, keeping the pairing between series [@wilks1997resampling]. Blocks were `r paste(sort(unique(vapply(as.integer(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15]), block_length, integer(1)))), collapse = ' or ')` seasons long for station records of `r min(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15])` to `r max(table(kept$station_name))` seasons, the cube root of the record length rounded up [@kunsch1989bootstrap], drawn in order of occurrence so that a gap fell inside a block. The interval on the difference was the percentile interval, and the two-sided p value, corrected for false discovery rate within the twelve metrics of one contrast at one station, followed the first guideline of @hall1991guidelines. The resampled differences were centred on the observed difference, and p was the share of them at least as far from it as the observed difference was from zero.

Daily ignition counts were modelled by negative binomial regression with a log link [@lawless1987negbin], in the daily form of @plucinski2014bushfires. The linear predictor contained the daily basin danger value, two annual harmonics in day of year after @martell1989seasonal, season as a factor and the number of stations contributing to the basin mean that day. The season factor gave each season its own intercept, so the danger coefficient was identified only from day-to-day variation inside a season, within which reporting completeness and cause coding did not change. The lightning model had no strike term, because the Canadian Lightning Detection Network climatology of @kochtubajda2020cldn covered only 1999 to 2018. Stationarity was tested by an interaction between the danger term and season number, the count form of the period by intensity interactions that @granville2022case fitted to industrial fires in Ontario from 1976 to 2019. The season effect followed @magnussen2012bc, whose year-specific British Columbia models showed coefficients varying between years "typically in excess of 100%" [@magnussen2012bc, p. 346].

Predictive skill was compared by the blocked cross-validation that @roberts2017crossvalidation recommended, in the leave-one-year-out form of @magnussen2012bc. Each season was left out in turn and scored by its log likelihood under the model refitted without it, the strictly proper logarithmic score of @gneiting2007scoring, comparable because the three series were scored on the same days. Because the three were close to transformations of one another, a small difference in held-out likelihood was not read as a difference in predictive power [@eastaugh2012cautionary].

Following @weatherhead1998detection, the minimum detectable trend for each metric over `r n_seasons` seasons was the slope at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 reached 80 per cent power, given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. The slope was adjusted for the lower efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator and inflated for serial correlation by the factor @weatherhead1998detection derived for first-order autoregressive noise, the square root of (1 + phi) / (1 − phi). Phi was the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals in season order, bounded between 0 and 0.9.

# Results {#sec-results}

```{r}
#| label: load-results
#| output: false
series_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-series-daily.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
series_daily$date <- as.Date(series_daily$date)
metrics <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "seasonal-metrics.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
thresh_pct <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "threshold-percentiles.csv"),
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "basin-daily.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin$date <- as.Date(basin$date)

# Relative-threshold counts are replaced by the in-base bootstrap estimates of
# Zhang et al. (2005), computed from the same daily series and the same
# 1991 to 2020 base period. Out-of-base seasons are unchanged by construction;
# the check below stops the render if any is not.
corrected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = c(90, 95),
                          reference = c(1991, 2020))))
for (pp in c(90, 95)) {
  col <- paste0("n_fwi_p", pp)
  cc <- corrected[corrected$prob == pp, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
  key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
  key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
  new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
  out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics[[col]])
  if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics[[col]][out_base]) > 1e-9))
    stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for ", col)
  metrics[[paste0(col, "_uncorrected")]] <- metrics[[col]]
  metrics[[col]] <- new
}
corrected_isi <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = 95,
                          reference = c(1991, 2020), component = "isi")))
cc <- corrected_isi[, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics$n_isi_p95)
if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics$n_isi_p95[out_base]) > 1e-9))
  stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for n_isi_p95")
metrics$n_isi_p95_uncorrected <- metrics$n_isi_p95
metrics$n_isi_p95 <- new
```

The checks of the FWI1987 implementation and of the hour at which each hourly series was reduced to one daily value were reported in Appendix A.

## Threshold Positions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Where each absolute threshold falls in each series' own 1991 to 2020 reference distribution, averaged over stations. A threshold at the same percentile in every series would mean the three systems are interchangeable for counting extremes. The reference median is the median of that component over the same distribution."
tp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(thresh_pct, list(thresh_pct$series, thresh_pct$component,
                         thresh_pct$threshold), drop = TRUE),
  function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Component = toupper(d$component[1]),
    Threshold = d$threshold[1],
    `Percentile of threshold` = round(mean(d$percentile_of_threshold, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days per season above` = NA_real_,
    `Reference median` = round(mean(d$reference_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
# Days per season above each absolute threshold, averaged over station-seasons.
days_above <- function(series, component, thr) {
  col <- switch(paste(component, thr),
                "ffmc 91" = "n_ffmc_ge91",
                "fwi 19" = "n_fwi_ge19",
                "fwi 30" = "n_fwi_ge30")
  mean(metrics[[col]][metrics$series == series], na.rm = TRUE)
}
key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(tp), "\\."))
tp$`Days per season above` <- round(mapply(days_above, key[, 1], key[, 2],
                                           as.numeric(key[, 3])), 1)
tp <- tp[order(tp$Component, tp$Threshold, tp$Series), ]
rownames(tp) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tp)
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-prose
#| output: false
ffmc91 <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
fwi19 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 19)
p_s1 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s2 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s3 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s1 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s2 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s3 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-reading
#| output: false
# The comparability claim is about where a value sits, so the reading is stated
# in the two units that matter and neither is rounded away: the percentile spread
# across series, and the difference in days per season an agency would count.
pct_spread <- max(abs(p_s3 - p_s1), abs(p_s2 - p_s1))
day_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
day_gap_pct <- 100 * day_gap / d_s1
```

Over the reference period of 1991 to 2020, the comparability sentence of @cffdg2025fwi2025, that a value under the 2025 version remained comparable with the same value under the 1987 version, was supported for levels and not for counts (@tbl-thresholds). The three reference medians of the Fine Fuel Moisture Code lay within about a unit of each other, and the three distributions almost coincided through the middle and separated near the threshold (@fig-distributions). A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 fell at the `r p_s1`th percentile of the S1 distribution, the `r p_s2`th of S2 and the `r p_s3`th of S3. The same threshold nonetheless selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` `r if (day_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under S3 than under S1, a difference of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(day_gap_pct))` per cent, because the percentile it occupied moved by `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_spread)` points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the daily Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the daily Fire Weather Index over all kept station-days under the three series, with the absolute thresholds marked. The comparability claim of the 2025 report concerns the position of a value on the scale; an extreme-day count concerns the mass beyond a threshold, which is a different quantity."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.75)
cols <- c(s1 = "#1B4F72", s2 = "#B7950B", s3 = "#943126")

plot_dens <- function(cols_prefix, xlab, cuts, xlim) {
  dens <- lapply(names(cols), function(s) {
    v <- series_daily[[paste0(s, "_", cols_prefix)]]
    density(v[is.finite(v)], na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  ymax <- max(vapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax * 1.05), xlab = xlab,
       ylab = "Density", main = "")
  for (i in seq_along(dens)) lines(dens[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 1.8)
  abline(v = cuts, lty = 3, col = "grey30")
  legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.8, bty = "n",
         cex = 0.72)
}
plot_dens("ffmc", "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", 91, c(40, 101))
plot_dens("fwi", "Fire Weather Index", c(19, 30), c(0, 60))
par(op)
```

## Mechanism

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003, under FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather and under FWI2025 driven by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days, and the only difference is the weather input the System received. The vertical lines mark 13:00 local daylight time, the hour FWI1987 observes, and 17:00, the hour a daily value conventionally represents."
ex <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "example-season-hourly.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ex$t <- as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:00:00", ex$yr, ex$mon, ex$day, ex$hr),
                   tz = "UTC")
win <- ex[ex$mon == 8 & ex$day >= 14 & ex$day <= 23, ]

op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, type = "l", col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6,
     ylim = range(c(win$s3_ffmc, win$s2_ffmc), na.rm = TRUE),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", xaxt = "n")
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
axis.POSIXct(1, win$t, format = "%d %b")
# The hour markers are drawn thin and pale on purpose: they locate the two
# sampling hours without competing with the curves, which are the subject.
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 12], col = "grey86", lty = 3, lwd = 0.6)
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 16], col = "grey62", lty = 2, lwd = 0.6)
lines(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6)
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(unname(SERIES[c("s3", "s2")]),
                  "13:00 LDT, the FWI1987 observation", "17:00 LDT"),
       col = c(cols["s3"], cols["s2"], "grey86", "grey62"),
       lwd = c(1.6, 1.6, 0.8, 0.8), lty = c(1, 1, 3, 2))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-capability
#| tbl-cap: "Two quantities FWI2025 reports and FWI1987 cannot, the hour at which peak burning conditions occur and the number of hours per day the burning window stays open, both as the specification's own daily summary computes them. Values are means over kept station-seasons. FWI1987 has no entry because a system with one value per day cannot say when in the day it applies."
cap <- metrics[metrics$series %in% c("s2", "s3") &
                 !is.na(metrics$mean_peak_hr), ]
if (nrow(cap)) {
  ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cap, cap$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Mean peak hour (LST)` = round(mean(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Mean burning window (h)` = round(mean(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Days per season with window >= 6 h` = round(mean(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(ct)
} else {
  stop("seasonal-metrics.csv carries no daily summary columns; re-run build_seasonal_metrics.py")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mechanism-reading
#| output: false
# The two readings the figure supports, computed from the same window it draws.
night <- win$hr %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)
day <- win$hr %in% c(14, 15, 16, 17)
night_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[night] - win$s2_ffmc[night], na.rm = TRUE)
day_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[day] - win$s2_ffmc[day], na.rm = TRUE)
range_s3 <- mean(tapply(win$s3_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
range_s2 <- mean(tapply(win$s2_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
```

At Penticton RS over ten days in August 2003, the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code under S2, reconstructed from the 13:00 observation, differed in shape from the code under S3 on the observed hourly weather (@fig-mechanism). The reconstructed code moved `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s2)` units between its daily minimum and maximum against `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s3)` for the observed series. The two ran `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` units apart in mid-afternoon and `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(night_gap))` units apart before dawn, so the reconstruction estimated the nights wetter than observed. @tbl-capability gave the consequence for the two quantities only the hourly system produced, the hour of peak burning conditions and the number of hours a day the burning window stayed open.

## Trends

```{r}
#| label: trend-compute
#| output: false
# The metric family. Each entry is a column of the seasonal metric table, a
# label, and which thresholding scheme it belongs to. The family is declared
# here, once, and the false discovery rate correction is applied within it.
METRICS <- data.frame(
  col = c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "peak_bui", "mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc",
          "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_ge30",
          "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95", "n_isi_p95"),
  label = c("Mean FWI", "Seasonal severity rating", "Peak BUI",
            "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC",
            "Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19", "Days FWI >= 30",
            "Days FWI above own 90th percentile",
            "Days FWI above own 95th percentile",
            "Days ISI above own 95th percentile"),
  scheme = c("level", "level", "level", "level", "level", "level",
             "absolute", "absolute", "absolute",
             "relative", "relative", "relative"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Trends are estimated per station and per series, then combined, rather than on
# a basin average, because the set of reporting stations changes between seasons
# and a basin average would move when a station joins or leaves.
trend_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      d <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == stn, ]
      d <- d[is.finite(d[[m]]), ]
      if (nrow(d) < 15) next
      tt <- trend_test(d$year, d[[m]])
      tt$series <- s; tt$metric <- m; tt$station <- stn
      tt$mdt <- minimum_detectable_trend(d$year, d[[m]])
      trend_rows[[length(trend_rows) + 1]] <- tt
    }
  }
}
trends <- do.call(rbind, trend_rows)
if (is.null(trends) || !nrow(trends))
  stop("No station has the 15 seasons the trend estimator requires. ",
       "Kept station-seasons: ", n_kept, " over ", n_seasons, " seasons. ",
       "Delete the weather record and the daily series and render again ",
       "to rebuild them over the full archive.")
# The family is the twelve metrics within one series at one station.
trends$q <- ave(trends$p_corrected,
                paste(trends$series, trends$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(trends, file.path(outputs, "trend-estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Theil-Sen slopes per season for each seasonal metric under each series, pooled across stations as the median station slope, with the range across stations. Significance is Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao variance correction; the count is of stations at which the false discovery rate adjusted p value falls below 0.05 within that station's twelve-metric family. The minimum detectable trend is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power."
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, list(trends$series, trends$metric),
                                  drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    Stations = nrow(d),
    `Median slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Slope range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE),
                            max(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Min detectable` = round(median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
tr <- tr[order(match(tr$Metric, METRICS$label), tr$Series), ]
rownames(tr) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tr)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 9.2
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal metrics by season under the three series, pooled across stations as the station mean, with the Theil-Sen line for each series. The absolute and relative extreme-day counts are the panels the second question turned on, under the prediction that the absolute counts separate between series and the relative counts do not."
show <- METRICS$col
# Generous bottom margin and tightened axis title placement: at four rows on one
# page the default margin clips the x axis label against the panel below.
op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 3), mar = c(3.8, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0),
          cex = 0.62)
for (m in show) {
  ylab <- METRICS$label[match(m, METRICS$col)]
  rng <- range(metrics[[m]], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(NA, xlim = range(metrics$year), ylim = rng, xlab = "Season", ylab = ylab,
       main = "")
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    d <- metrics[metrics$series == s, ]
    a <- aggregate(d[[m]], list(year = d$year), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    points(a$year, a$x, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
    sl <- theil_sen(a$year, a$x)
    ic <- median(a$x - sl * a$year)
    abline(a = ic, b = sl, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
  }
  if (m == show[1])
    legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, bty = "n",
           cex = 0.7)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: trend-reading
#| output: false
# The direction and strength of the trend picture, computed rather than eyeballed
# off the table, so the sentence below cannot say something the numbers do not.
tr_up <- sum(trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_n <- sum(is.finite(trends$slope))
tr_sig <- sum(trends$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_sig_up <- sum(trends$q < 0.05 & trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
# What the autocorrelation correction changed, in tests that would pass on the
# uncorrected variance, corrected within the same families as the reported q
# values, each station's twelve metrics within a series.
would_pass <- sum(unlist(lapply(split(trends$p_uncorrected, list(trends$series, trends$station), drop = TRUE),
  function(p) p.adjust(p, "BH"))) < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
infl <- median(trends$n_over_nstar, na.rm = TRUE)
# The two extremes among the extreme-day counts, which share the unit days per
# season, so that the paragraph names its highest and lowest cases rather than
# reporting only a count of how many passed.
day_tr <- trends[trends$metric %in% METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme != "level"], ]
hi <- day_tr[which.max(day_tr$slope), ]
lo <- day_tr[which.min(day_tr$slope), ]
name_case <- function(r) sprintf("%s under %s at %s (%+.2f days per season, 95 per cent interval %+.2f to %+.2f, q = %s)",
  METRICS$label[match(r$metric, METRICS$col)], unname(SERIES_PROSE[r$series]),
  station_prose(r$station),
  r$slope, r$lower, r$upper, ifelse(r$q < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", r$q)))
```

Across the study window, `r tr_up` of the `r tr_n` station, series and metric combinations at the `r length(unique(trends$station))` stations with at least 15 usable seasons had a positive Theil-Sen slope (@tbl-trends, @fig-trends). After the Hamed and Rao variance correction and the false discovery rate correction within each station's twelve-metric family, `r tr_sig` combinations had a q value below 0.05, `r tr_sig_up` of them positive. The median ratio of the nominal to the effective sample size, the number of independent seasons the correlated record was worth, was `r sprintf("%.2f", infl)`, and on the uncorrected variance `r would_pass` combinations would have passed the same threshold. Among the extreme-day counts, which shared the unit days per season, the steepest rise was in `r name_case(hi)` and the `r if (lo$slope < 0) "steepest fall" else "shallowest rise"` in `r name_case(lo)`.

## Version Dependence

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-compute
#| output: false
CONTRASTS <- list(
  c("s1", "s2", "Version change, input held at 13:00"),
  c("s2", "s3", "Input resolution change, version held at FWI2025"),
  c("s1", "s3", "Operational migration, both changes")
)

diff_rows <- list()
for (cn in CONTRASTS) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      a <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[1] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      b <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[2] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      w <- merge(a, b, by = "year", suffixes = c(".a", ".b"))
      names(w)[2:3] <- c("a", "b")
      if (nrow(w) < 15) next
      sd_ <- slope_difference(w)
      sd_$contrast <- cn[3]; sd_$metric <- m; sd_$station <- stn
      sd_$scheme <- METRICS$scheme[i]
      diff_rows[[length(diff_rows) + 1]] <- sd_
    }
  }
}
sdiff <- do.call(rbind, diff_rows)
if (is.null(sdiff) || !nrow(sdiff))
  stop("No station-series pair has the 15 paired seasons the bootstrap requires.")
# The family here is the twelve metrics within one contrast at one station: one
# station's answer to one of the three questions the design asks.
sdiff$q <- ave(sdiff$p_two_sided, paste(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(sdiff, file.path(outputs, "slope-differences.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-slopediff
#| tbl-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series, by metric and contrast, pooled across stations as the median. Intervals are paired moving-block bootstrap percentile intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons, which preserves both the dependence between series that share a weather record and the serial correlation within each. Stations excluding zero counts the stations whose own interval does not contain zero; the last column applies the Benjamini and Hochberg correction within each station's twelve-metric family for that contrast."
sd_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(sdiff, list(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$metric), drop = TRUE), function(d) {
    data.frame(
      Contrast = d$contrast[1],
      Scheme = d$scheme[1],
      Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
      Stations = nrow(d),
      `Median difference` = round(median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      `Stations excluding zero` = sum(d$lower > 0 | d$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      check.names = FALSE)
  }))
sd_tab <- sd_tab[order(match(sd_tab$Contrast, vapply(CONTRASTS, `[`, "", 3)),
                       match(sd_tab$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(sd_tab) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(sd_tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-slopediff
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series for the six extreme-day counts, which all measure days per season and therefore share one axis. Points are station estimates, bars are paired moving-block bootstrap 95 per cent intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons. Red marks the three absolute thresholds and blue the three thresholds internal to each series. The prediction under test is that the red points separate from zero and the blue ones do not. The six level metrics are omitted from this figure because the seasonal severity rating and the Drought Code are measured on scales two orders of magnitude larger and would compress everything else to a point; they are in the preceding table."
# Only the metrics measured in days per season are drawn, so one x axis means the
# same thing everywhere on the figure. A common range across the three panels
# keeps the contrasts comparable, and the labels are drawn once on the left.
DAY_METRICS <- METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme %in% c("absolute", "relative")]
sd_plot <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% DAY_METRICS, ]
sd_plot$mi <- match(sd_plot$metric, METRICS$col)
xr <- range(c(sd_plot$lower, sd_plot$upper, 0), na.rm = TRUE)

# The left outer margin is sized from the longest row label, so that a longer
# metric name cannot clip the labels as a fixed width did on 2026-10-26.
lab_w <- max(nchar(paste0(METRICS$label[sd_plot$mi], ", ", sd_plot$station)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), oma = c(1.6, 0.31 * lab_w, 0, 0), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (k in seq_along(CONTRASTS)) {
  cn <- CONTRASTS[[k]]
  d <- sd_plot[sd_plot$contrast == cn[3], ]
  par(mar = c(2.6, 0.6, 3.4, 0.6))
  if (!nrow(d)) { plot.new(); next }
  d <- d[order(d$mi, d$station), ]
  y <- seq_len(nrow(d))
  plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0.5, max(y) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = paste(strwrap(cn[3], 24), collapse = "\n"), cex.main = 0.95)
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  segments(d$lower, y, d$upper, y, col = "grey35")
  points(d$difference, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         col = ifelse(d$scheme == "absolute", "#943126", "#1B4F72"))
  if (k == 1)
    axis(2, at = y, labels = paste0(METRICS$label[d$mi], ", ", d$station),
         las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7, tick = FALSE, line = -0.3, outer = TRUE)
}
# One axis title under all three panels, because the panels share the axis and
# three titles side by side ran into one another.
mtext("Slope difference, days per season", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.3, cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-reading
#| output: false
# The hypothesis has a specific shape: absolute-threshold counts should separate
# between series and relative-threshold counts should not. That shape is scored
# here as two rates, so the sentence below reports what the numbers show rather
# than what the hypothesis predicted.
score <- function(contrast, scheme) {
  d <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == contrast & sdiff$scheme == scheme, ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(c(n = 0, sig = 0, rate = NA_real_, med = NA_real_))
  sig <- sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  c(n = nrow(d), sig = sig, rate = 100 * sig / nrow(d),
    med = median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE))
}
ver_label <- CONTRASTS[[1]][3]
inp_label <- CONTRASTS[[2]][3]
mig_label <- CONTRASTS[[3]][3]
sc <- rbind(
  `version, absolute`   = score(ver_label, "absolute"),
  `version, relative`   = score(ver_label, "relative"),
  `input, absolute`     = score(inp_label, "absolute"),
  `input, relative`     = score(inp_label, "relative"),
  `migration, absolute` = score(mig_label, "absolute"),
  `migration, relative` = score(mig_label, "relative"))
sc <- as.data.frame(sc)
write.csv(sc, file.path(outputs, "hypothesis-scoring.csv"))

# The resolution of the difference test, so that a null is readable. The half
# width of the bootstrap interval is the smallest difference this record could
# have separated from zero at each station and metric.
sdiff$halfwidth <- (sdiff$upper - sdiff$lower) / 2
res_abs <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "absolute"], na.rm = TRUE)
res_rel <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "relative"], na.rm = TRUE)
n_any_sig <- sum(sdiff$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
verdict <- if (!is.finite(abs_rate) || !is.finite(rel_rate)) {
  "could not be scored"
} else if (abs_rate == 0 && rel_rate == 0) {
  "divergence under neither scheme, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism"
} else if (abs_rate > rel_rate) {
  "the pattern the mechanism predicted"
} else if (abs_rate > 0) {
  "divergence under both schemes, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism"
} else {
  "divergence under the percentile scheme alone, the opposite of the pattern the mechanism predicted"
}
```

Across the study window, the migration contrast, S1 against S3, gave `r verdict`. The absolute-threshold metrics gave a slope difference excluding zero at `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of station and metric combinations against `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, relative", "rate"])` per cent for the relative-threshold metrics (@tbl-slopediff, @fig-slopediff). Across all `r nrow(sdiff)` station, metric and contrast combinations, `r n_any_sig` gave a slope difference with a corrected p value below 0.05. The resolution of the test, the median half width of the bootstrap intervals on the slope differences, was `r sprintf("%.3f", res_abs)` days per season for the absolute-threshold metrics and `r sprintf("%.3f", res_rel)` for the relative ones. Over the `r yr_last - yr_first` season window that was `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", res_rel * (yr_last - yr_first))` days respectively. When the migration contrast was split into its two halves, the version change alone, S1 against S2, gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["version, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of absolute-metric slope differences excluding zero and the input resolution change alone, S2 against S3, gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["input, absolute", "rate"])` per cent. The median differences were `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["version, absolute", "med"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["input, absolute", "med"])` per season respectively against `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["migration, absolute", "med"])` for the two together.

## Ignition Skill

```{r}
#| label: ignition-compute
#| output: false
mod_dat <- merge(basin, ign_daily, by = c("date", "year", "doy"))
mod_dat <- mod_dat[format(mod_dat$date, "%m") %in% c("05", "06", "07", "08", "09"), ]

SKILL_RESPONSES <- c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")

RESPONSES <- c(n_lightning_all = "Lightning, no size limit",
               n_person_all = "Person, no size limit",
               n_total_all = "All causes, no size limit",
               n_total_ge1ha = "All causes, at least 1 ha",
               n_total_ge4ha = "All causes, at least 4 ha")

ign_rows <- list()
for (r in names(RESPONSES)) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    if (!dcol %in% names(mod_dat)) next
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, r, dcol, extra = "n_stations"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    # Held-out skill is computed only for the two responses the comparison
    # between series is read from. It refits the model once per season, so
    # running it on all five responses costs several hundred fits for numbers
    # the text does not use, and the cost is reported rather than hidden.
    sk <- if (r %in% SKILL_RESPONSES)
      tryCatch(loso_skill(mod_dat, r, dcol), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
    # Wald interval on the danger coefficient rather than a profile likelihood
    # one. Profiling a negative binomial with a factor per season means refitting
    # once per grid point per model, which dominated the render, and the two
    # agree closely at this sample size. The interval is reported as Wald.
    se <- summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 2]
    ci <- coef(m)[".x"] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
    ign_rows[[length(ign_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      coef = unname(coef(m)[".x"]),
      lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
      p = summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 4],
      theta = m$theta,
      loso_loglik = if (is.null(sk)) NA_real_ else sk$mean_loglik,
      n_days = nrow(mod_dat))
  }
}
ign_res <- do.call(rbind, ign_rows)
write.csv(ign_res, file.path(outputs, "ignition-models.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ignition
#| tbl-cap: "Negative binomial models of daily ignition counts on daily basin Fire Weather Index, over the 1 May to 30 September window, with season as a fixed effect, two annual harmonics in day of year, and the number of contributing stations. The coefficient is the log change in expected count per unit of Fire Weather Index, identified from within-season variation only. Held-out log likelihood is the mean per day under leave-one-season-out refitting; larger is better, and the comparison between series rather than its absolute value is the quantity of interest. It is computed for the lightning and all-cause responses only, because those are the two the text compares and each refits the model once per season."
it <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[ign_res$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[ign_res$series]),
  `Coefficient` = round(ign_res$coef, 4),
  `95% Wald interval` = sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", ign_res$lower, ign_res$upper),
  `Rate ratio per 10 FWI` = round(exp(10 * ign_res$coef), 2),
  `Held-out log likelihood` = round(ign_res$loso_loglik, 4),
  check.names = FALSE)
it <- it[order(match(it$Response, unname(RESPONSES)), it$Series), ]
rownames(it) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(it)
```

```{r}
#| label: ignition-prose
#| output: false
best <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
best <- best[order(-best$loso_loglik), ]
skill_gap <- diff(range(best$loso_loglik))

# Does the danger term survive at every size threshold, and does it separate the
# lightning series from the person-caused control? The control matters: human
# ignition tracks population and access, so a danger signal appearing equally in
# both would point to a shared confounder rather than to fuel moisture.
sig_by_response <- tapply(ign_res$p, ign_res$response, function(p) sum(p < 0.05))
rr <- function(resp, s) {
  v <- ign_res$coef[ign_res$response == resp & ign_res$series == s]
  if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else exp(10 * v)
}
rr_light <- rr("n_lightning_all", "s3")
rr_person <- rr("n_person_all", "s3")
```

Over the summer window, the danger term in the negative binomial ignition models, the coefficient on the daily basin Fire Weather Index, was positive with a p value below 0.05 for `r sum(ign_res$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r nrow(ign_res)` response and series combinations (@tbl-ignition). The person-caused response was significant under every series and the lightning response only under FWI1987. Under FWI2025 on hourly weather, ten units of Fire Weather Index multiplied the expected daily person-caused count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_person)` and the expected daily lightning count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_light)`. Under FWI1987 the fitted dispersion parameter was `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"][1])` for the lightning series against `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_person_all"][1])` for the person-caused one, a smaller value meaning more clustered counts.

The difference in predictive skill between series, the third question, was small. On held-out seasons, the three series differed by `r sprintf("%.4f", skill_gap)` in mean log likelihood per day for lightning ignitions, with `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[1]])` first at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[1])` and `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[nrow(best)]])` last at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[nrow(best)])`. Over the `r format(best$n_days[1], big.mark = ",")` days in the window that was a total of about `r sprintf("%.1f", skill_gap * best$n_days[1])` log likelihood units (@fig-ignition).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ignition
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Observed and fitted daily lightning ignition rate against daily basin Fire Weather Index under the three series. Points are the observed mean count in equal-count bins of the danger value; lines are the fitted negative binomial rate at the mean season and the mid-season day of year. The horizontal offsets between the three curves are the same level differences that the threshold table reports as percentiles."
# Two things are drawn and they are different. The points are the observed mean
# daily count in equal-count bins of the danger value, so each rests on the same
# number of days and the right hand tail is not one noisy observation. The curves
# are the fitted negative binomial rate, refitted here for the lightning response,
# evaluated at the mean fitted season effect and at mid-season day of year, which
# is what the model says a typical season looks like.
binned <- lapply(names(SERIES), function(s) {
  x <- mod_dat[[paste0(s, "_fwi")]]
  y <- mod_dat$n_lightning_all
  ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  br <- unique(quantile(x[ok], seq(0, 1, length.out = 13), na.rm = TRUE))
  bin <- cut(x[ok], br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  data.frame(x = tapply(x[ok], bin, mean), y = tapply(y[ok], bin, mean))
})
names(binned) <- names(SERIES)

mid_doy <- median(mod_dat$doy)
fitted_curve <- function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, "n_lightning_all", paste0(s, "_fwi"),
                               extra = "n_stations"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  co <- coef(m)
  cf <- function(nm) if (nm %in% names(co) && is.finite(co[[nm]])) co[[nm]] else 0
  yr_terms <- co[grepl("^\\.year", names(co))]
  grid <- seq(min(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE), max(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE),
              length.out = 60)
  eta <- cf("(Intercept)") + mean(c(0, yr_terms), na.rm = TRUE) + cf(".x") * grid +
    cf(".s1") * sin(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c1") * cos(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".s2") * sin(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c2") * cos(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf("n_stations") * mean(mod_dat$n_stations)
  data.frame(x = grid, y = exp(eta))
}
curves <- lapply(names(SERIES), fitted_curve)
names(curves) <- names(SERIES)

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.8)
plot(NA,
     xlim = range(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "x")), na.rm = TRUE),
     ylim = c(0, max(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "y")), na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Daily basin Fire Weather Index",
     ylab = "Mean lightning ignitions per day")
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  points(binned[[s]]$x, binned[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.8)
  if (!is.null(curves[[s]])) lines(curves[[s]]$x, curves[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
}
legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, pch = 16,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: stationarity
#| output: false
# Is the danger to ignition relationship stationary? The test is an interaction
# between the danger term and season number. Season is already a fixed effect,
# so the interaction asks whether the within-season slope changes over the
# record, which is a different question from whether the intercept does.
stat_rows <- list()
for (r in c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    d <- mod_dat
    d$.yc <- d$year - mean(d$year)
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(d, r, dcol, extra = "I(.x * .yc)"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
    nm <- grep("I\\(.x", rownames(cf), value = TRUE)[1]
    stat_rows[[length(stat_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      interaction = cf[nm, 1], se = cf[nm, 2], p = cf[nm, 4])
  }
}
stationarity <- do.call(rbind, stat_rows)
write.csv(stationarity, file.path(outputs, "stationarity-tests.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stationarity
#| tbl-cap: "Test of whether the within-season relationship between fire danger and daily ignition count changes across the record. The reported term is the interaction between the Fire Weather Index and centred season number; a positive value would mean more ignitions per unit danger in later seasons. Season is already a fixed effect, so this asks about the slope and not the level."
st <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[stationarity$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[stationarity$series]),
  `Interaction` = signif(stationarity$interaction, 3),
  `Standard error` = signif(stationarity$se, 3),
  `p` = signif(stationarity$p, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(st)
```

Across the record, `r sum(stationarity$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r nrow(stationarity)` interaction terms between the danger term and season number, the test of whether the danger to ignition relationship changed with time, had a p value below 0.05 (@tbl-stationarity).

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: discussion-numbers
#| output: false
# The level shifts each change produces, per season, on the two absolute-threshold
# counts and on the three level metrics whose equations the 2025 revision rewrote.
# Sign matters here and is computed, not asserted: the two changes do not
# necessarily push the same way.
lvl <- function(metric, a, b) {
  mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == b], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == a], na.rm = TRUE)
}
shift_cols <- c("n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc")
shift <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19", "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC"),
  unit = c("days", "days", "ISI units", "DMC units", "DC units"),
  version = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s1", b = "s2"),
  input = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s2", b = "s3"),
  migration = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s1", b = "s3"),
  row.names = NULL
)
# The migration shift as a share of the FWI1987 level of the same metric.
base_s1 <- sapply(shift_cols, function(m) mean(metrics[[m]][metrics$series == "s1"], na.rm = TRUE))
shift$migration_pct <- 100 * shift$migration / base_s1
write.csv(shift, file.path(outputs, "level-shifts.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Direction words for the prose, computed so a sentence cannot assert a sign the
# numbers do not show. Rows 3 to 5 are the spread index and the two slow codes.
up_down <- function(x, up = "raised", down = "lowered") if (x >= 0) up else down
slow_verdict <- if (all(shift$version[4:5] > 0)) {
  "the dry side the report predicted for its cumulative rain thresholds"
} else "not the dry side the report predicted for its cumulative rain thresholds"
slow_phrase <- if (all(shift$version[4:5] > 0)) "the slow codes to the dry side" else
  if (all(shift$version[4:5] < 0)) "the slow codes to the wet side" else
  "the slow codes in opposite directions"
# Slope differences excluding zero among the four metrics added for the rewritten
# components, over all three contrasts.
new_metric_names <- c("mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc", "n_isi_p95",
                      "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC", "Days ISI above own 95th percentile")
sd_new <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% new_metric_names, ]
stopifnot(nrow(sd_new) == 4 * length(unique(sdiff$station)) * length(unique(sdiff$contrast)))
n_excl_new <- sum(sd_new$lower > 0 | sd_new$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
excl_word <- if (n_excl_new == 0) "None" else as.character(n_excl_new)

same_sign <- function(i) sign(shift$version[i]) == sign(shift$input[i])
ffmc_word <- if (same_sign(1)) "compounded" else "opposed one another"
fwi_word <- if (same_sign(2)) "compounded" else "opposed one another"

# Where the two changes oppose, what survives is the residual, and how much
# survives is the whole point. Cancellation is measured as the migration shift
# relative to the larger of the two component shifts.
residual <- function(i) {
  abs(shift$migration[i]) / max(abs(shift$version[i]), abs(shift$input[i]))
}
ffmc_res <- residual(1); fwi_res <- residual(2)
bigger <- function(i) if (abs(shift$version[i]) > abs(shift$input[i]))
  "the version change" else "the input resolution change"
```

In the Okanagan basin of British Columbia, the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System was run as three series on one weather record, one pair isolating the version change and the other the change in input resolution. The revision moved the count of extreme days and moved no trend this record could resolve. The predicted divergence in slope appeared under neither thresholding scheme, which refuted the mechanism, and the three series were barely distinguishable in their skill at predicting daily ignitions.

## Version and Input

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shift
#| tbl-cap: "How each change moved the level of each metric, averaged over kept station-seasons, in the metric's own unit. The version column is FWI1987 to FWI2025 at fixed 13:00 input; the input column is the 13:00 reconstruction to observed hourly weather at fixed FWI2025; the migration column is both, and equals their sum by construction."
sh <- data.frame(
  Metric = shift$metric,
  Unit = shift$unit,
  `Version change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version),
  `Input resolution change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input),
  `Migration, both` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(sh)
```

@tbl-shift shows that the two changes were large and pointed opposite ways, so a straight comparison of FWI1987 against FWI2025 would have been uninterpretable. On the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, the version change moved the seasonal count by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[1])` days and the input resolution change by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[1])`, so the two `r ffmc_word` and `r bigger(1)` won. The migration, both changes together, netted `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days. On the count of days above a Fire Weather Index of 19, the two changes moved it by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` days, so there they `r fwi_word` almost exactly. The migration netted `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` days on that count, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fwi_res)` per cent of the larger component. That near cancellation was a coincidence of two large effects at one place, not to be expected at a site with a different diurnal range, the difference in temperature and humidity between night and day.

The two changes did not move the counts in the directions expected. The version change halved the fine fuel time lag, yet it lowered the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 and raised the count above a Fire Weather Index of 19, and the input change did the reverse. At five stations in the Alps, differences between regions were largest in the Fine Fuel Moisture Code, smaller in the Duff Moisture Code and smallest in the Drought Code, an order @wastl2013large attributed to the time lags of the fuel layers each code represents. A halved fine fuel time lag should therefore have acted most strongly on the Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the counts built from it, which this record did not show. @rodrigues2020identifying noted that the same Fire Weather Index value could arise from different combinations of weather variables, so two changes acting on different parts of the calculation could offset in the combined index while remaining visible in its parts.

At fixed 13:00 input, FWI2025 `r up_down(shift$version[4])` the mean Duff Moisture Code by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$version[4]))` units and `r up_down(shift$version[5])` the peak Drought Code by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$version[5]))` units over FWI1987, `r slow_verdict` [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 21]. The hourly input then `r up_down(shift$input[4])` the Duff Moisture Code by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$input[4]))` units and moved the Drought Code by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[5])`, so the migration netted a Duff Moisture Code `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration_pct[4]))` per cent `r up_down(shift$migration[4], "higher", "lower")` and a Drought Code `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration_pct[5]))` per cent `r up_down(shift$migration[5], "higher", "lower")` than under FWI1987. The mean Initial Spread Index `r up_down(shift$version[3], "rose", "fell")` by `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(shift$version[3]))` under the version change despite the new wind cap, consistent with a 16:00 daily value taken nearer the afternoon peak than the 13:00 observation, and the hourly input moved it by `r sprintf("%+.2f", shift$input[3])`. `r excl_word` of the four metrics added for the rewritten components had a slope difference that excluded zero in any contrast.

On thirteen years of station data from Camden, New South Wales, the differences in structure between three fire danger systems partly cancelled once each used its own observation time and moisture sub-models [@matthews2009comparison], as the version and input effects did here for days above a Fire Weather Index of 19. That study followed no trend through the change. The one measured effect of input timing on a slope was the 0.22 to 0.39 days per decade by which daily aggregates inflated a global extreme-day trend [@matteo2025challenges]. Over this window that would have amounted to `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.22 * (yr_last - yr_first) / 10)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.39 * (yr_last - yr_first) / 10)` days, against the `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days this record could resolve, so the null slope result bounded the effect rather than excluding it.

The clearest difference between the two FWI2025 series was not in any level but in the burning window. Both series followed the report's own procedures, so an agency that migrated to FWI2025 while still supplying a 13:00 observation would receive outputs computed from an assumed diurnal curve. A daily index cannot say when the peak arrives or how long it lasts, the two quantities a decision on initial attack, the first response to a new fire, needs. The hourly series reported them without predicting ignitions better.

The small difference in ignition skill between series was consistent with comparisons of danger indices against fire records elsewhere. In Mediterranean France, the Fire Weather Index was the most skilful of the indices tested, but no index alone was sufficient to rate fire activity without spatial and seasonal effects [@castelclavera2025comparative]. The models here included the seasonal effect, and a model of one basin mean had no spatial effect to include. Models tested across 11 regions from the European Alps to the Mediterranean basin that ranked fire occurrence well could still perform poorly on burned area [@bekar2023integrating], so the ignition counts tested here could not show whether the three series would differ on area burned.

## Published Trends

Because the migration changed no estimated trend at any station under either thresholding scheme, the consequence for the published record rested on the level result alone, and it was narrow. Trends reported as percentile exceedances were largely unaffected by the version change, because the threshold moved with the distribution. Trends reported as counts above a fixed danger class were not, and neither were seasonal severity ratings, which summed a function of the index over a season and so inherited any level shift. A percentile trend was portable across the version change only when its reference period was stated, kept fixed and corrected for the base-period bias.

Nothing here showed the published trends to be wrong, but they were statements about FWI1987, and restating them under FWI2025 would change some by an amount set by the metric's definition rather than by the weather. A level shift that did not alter the relative change had been reported before in this index, when @quilcaille2023fire found that computing the Fire Weather Index from mean rather than minimum humidity reduced it "by about −33 % (June) above 20° N" [@quilcaille2023fire, p. 2162] while the reduction was "roughly identical during the fire seasons across the planet, be it over 1994–2014 or 2081–2100" [@quilcaille2023fire, p. 2164]. @mortelmans2024peatland instead "matched the temporal cumulative density functions (CDFs) of the PEATCLSM output variables" to those of the moisture codes in each grid cell [@mortelmans2024peatland, p. 448]. That step kept the percentile of a day fixed within the matching period, and so the counts above percentile thresholds, while leaving the absolute counts to move, the same split between the two threshold families reported here. A historical trend re-expressed in the new system's units should therefore be recomputed over the whole record rather than joined across the change, and reported with its metric family.

## Limitations

```{r}
#| label: limits-compute
#| output: false
# The quantitative limits statement. For each metric the minimum detectable trend
# is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power, given the residual
# spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. Expressing it over the whole
# window rather than per season is what makes it legible: a slope of 0.3 days per
# season is 10 days over 34 seasons, and the second number is the one a reader can
# judge.
lim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, trends$metric), function(d) {
  mdt <- median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    `Median observed slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Minimum detectable slope` = round(mdt, 3),
    `Minimum detectable change over the window` =
      round(mdt * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    `Observed change over the window` =
      round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE) * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
lim <- lim[order(match(lim$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(lim) <- NULL
write.csv(lim, file.path(outputs, "detectability.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-limits
#| tbl-cap: "What a window of this length can and cannot resolve. The minimum detectable slope is the trend at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator relative to least squares and inflated for lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals. A metric whose observed change is smaller than its minimum detectable change is not evidence of no trend; it is evidence that this record cannot see one of that size."
fmt_tbl(lim)
```

@tbl-limits gives the quantitative form of what this study could not say, because a null result and an underpowered result looked identical in a table of p values and were different claims.

The study covered only the Canadian part of one basin, so whether the version effect had the same size elsewhere was untested. The study detected change and did not attribute it, because attribution requires a comparison against a world without anthropogenic forcing, the human contribution to climate change [@kirchmeieryoung2019attribution]. Two further limits applied to the absolute trends and not to the comparison between series, because whatever moved one series moved all three. No index of the El Niño Southern Oscillation or the Pacific Decadal Oscillation entered any model, so a window that began and ended in different phases of those oscillations biased the absolute trends. The sensor history of the stations was not available, and in the national network @vanwijngaarden2005examination found that replacing the psychrometer by the dewcel "produced a decreasing step in relative humidity at a number of stations" [@vanwijngaarden2005examination, abstract]. Fuel typing did not vary through time, so a danger effect was not distinguished from fuel accumulation, and in Bavaria meteorological fire danger rose while the number of fires and the area burned fell [@wastl2012climate]. The fixed window from 1 May to 30 September could not register a season that lengthened at either end, so if the true season lengthened, trends in window counts understated trends in the season.

A year-round climate station of the kind @hanes2020overwinter used would recover the season from this basin and would allow the Drought Code to be overwintered rather than restarted each spring, a restart @mcelhinny2020era5 showed changed the count of spread days.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

```{r}
#| label: conclusions-numbers
#| output: false
# The four numbers the conclusions rest on, pulled from the objects above rather
# than retyped.
c_days_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
c_pct_gap <- 100 * c_days_gap / d_s1
c_dur <- if (exists("ct") && nrow(ct) == 2) {
  ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S3", ct$Series)] -
    ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S2", ct$Series)]
} else NA_real_
c_abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
c_rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
```

Over `r n_seasons` seasons in the Okanagan basin, the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System was run in its 1987 and 2025 versions on one record. A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, the 2025 report's example of continuity, selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(c_days_gap))` `r if (c_days_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under FWI2025 on hourly weather than under FWI1987, a change of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(c_pct_gap))` per cent. The migration changed the estimated trend at `r sprintf("%.0f", c_abs_rate)` per cent of station-metric combinations under fixed thresholds and at `r sprintf("%.0f", c_rel_rate)` per cent under percentile thresholds, `r verdict`. The refutation extended down to a slope divergence of about `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days over the window, the resolution of this record. The three fuel moisture codes and the spread index, recomputed under the 2025 equations, shifted in level, `r slow_phrase`, `r if (n_excl_new == 0) "and in no case changed a trend this record could resolve" else sprintf("and changed a trend in %d of their slope differences", n_excl_new)`.

Fire danger trends should therefore be reported as days above a percentile of the series itself, not as counts above a fixed danger class, because the percentile moved with its distribution across the version change and the class boundary did not. The reference period should be stated, fixed and corrected for the base-period bias. The recommendation rested on the level result in one basin, and the study attributed no change to a cause. For daily ignition counts the three series were close to interchangeable, but on the burning window the observed hourly weather and the reconstructed diurnal curve disagreed by `r if (is.finite(c_dur)) sprintf("%.1f hours per day", c_dur) else "an amount this run did not compute"`. An agency migrating to FWI2025 on a 13:00 observation alone would inherit that difference with no sign of it in the output.

# Appendix A. Review and checks {#sec-appendix-review .unnumbered}

## A.1 Literature Review {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: review-terms
#| output: false
# Search terms come only from the manuscript's own title and keywords, so a reader
# can trace every term to the front matter. Candidates are written once; the
# selection is typed into the file and never overwritten by a render.
if (!file.exists("../04.references/review/search-terms.csv")) {
  front <- rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(knitr::current_input())
  small <- c("a", "an", "and", "as", "at", "by", "do", "does", "for", "from", "how", "in", "into", "is", "its", "of", "on", "or", "the", "to", "under", "using", "versus", "what", "why", "with")
  phrases <- \(x) x |>
    stringr::str_to_lower() |>
    stringr::str_remove_all("[*_]") |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]-]", " | ") |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(paste0("\\b(", paste(small, collapse = "|"), ")\\b"), " | ") |>
    stringr::str_split_1("\\|") |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    purrr::keep(\(p) nchar(p) > 2)
  dir.create("../04.references/review", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    tibble::tibble(term = stringr::str_squish(stringr::str_to_lower(unlist(stringr::str_split(unlist(front$keywords), "[;,]")))), source = "keywords"),
    tibble::tibble(term = phrases(front$title), source = "title"),
    tibble::tibble(term = phrases(front$subtitle %||% ""), source = "subtitle")
  ) |>
    dplyr::distinct(term, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::mutate(question = NA, concept = NA) |>
    readr::write_csv("../04.references/review/search-terms.csv", na = "")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: review-queries
#| output: false
front <- rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(knitr::current_input())
declared <- paste(front$title, front$subtitle, paste(unlist(front$keywords), collapse = " ")) |>
  stringr::str_remove_all("[*_]") |>
  stringr::str_to_lower()
term_regex <- \(x) if (stringr::str_ends(x, "\\*")) paste0("\\b", stringr::str_escape(stringr::str_remove(x, "\\*$"))) else paste0("\\b", stringr::str_escape(x), "\\b")
terms <- readr::read_csv("../04.references/review/search-terms.csv", col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c")) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(question), !is.na(concept)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(term = stringr::str_to_lower(term)) |>
  tidyr::separate_longer_delim(question, " ")
stray <- terms$term[!purrr::map_lgl(terms$term, \(x) stringr::str_detect(declared, term_regex(x)))]
if (nrow(terms) == 0) stop("No search terms selected in 04.references/review/search-terms.csv")
if (length(stray) > 0) stop("Not in the title, subtitle or keywords: ", paste(unique(stray), collapse = ", "))
queries <- terms |>
  dplyr::summarise(.by = c(question, concept), group = paste(term, collapse = "|")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(.by = question, route = paste(c(dplyr::first(question), concept), collapse = "-"), concepts = paste(group, collapse = " AND "))
# One boolean string per query for the external indexes. A term ending in * is a
# stem; the external indexes stem on their own, so the star is dropped there.
boolean_query <- function(concepts, or = " OR ", and = " AND ") {
  stringr::str_split_1(concepts, " AND ") |>
    purrr::map_chr(\(g) paste0("(", paste(purrr::map_chr(stringr::str_split_1(g, "\\|"), \(x) {
      x <- stringr::str_remove(x, "\\*$")
      if (grepl(" ", x)) paste0('"', x, '"') else x
    }), collapse = or), ")")) |>
    paste(collapse = and)
}
# A query is sent to a source once. The search log names every query a source
# has answered, so a later pass sends only the queries added to the terms file
# since the pass before, and each pass extends the log and the hits files rather
# than replacing them.
search_log_path <- "../02.inputs/derived/review-search-log.csv"
read_search_log <- function() if (file.exists(search_log_path)) readr::read_csv(search_log_path, col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c")) else tibble::tibble(strand = character(), route = character())
pending_queries <- function(prefix) queries[!paste0(prefix, queries$route) %in% read_search_log()$route, ]
append_csv <- function(rows, path) {
  rows <- dplyr::mutate(rows, dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), as.character))
  old <- if (file.exists(path)) readr::read_csv(path, col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c")) else NULL
  readr::write_csv(dplyr::bind_rows(old, rows), path)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: review-store
#| output: false
pending <- pending_queries("store-")
if (nrow(pending) > 0) {
  # library-science manifest, https://github.com/seamusrobertmurphy/library-science/blob/main/library/manifest.csv
  manifest <- readr::read_csv("../../library-science/library/manifest.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  # library-science source notes, https://github.com/seamusrobertmurphy/library-science/tree/main/sources
  notes <- tibble::tibble(path = list.files("../../library-science/sources", "\\.md$", full.names = TRUE)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(key = tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(path)), note = purrr::map_chr(path, \(p) paste(readLines(p, warn = FALSE), collapse = " ")))
  store <- manifest |>
    dplyr::filter(status %in% c("verified", "filed", "unverified"), !is.na(title) | !is.na(key)) |>
    dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(notes, key, note), by = "key") |>
    dplyr::mutate(text = stringr::str_to_lower(paste(title, note)))
  hits <- pending |>
    purrr::pmap(\(question, route, concepts) {
      groups <- stringr::str_split_1(concepts, " AND ")
      term <- \(x) if (stringr::str_ends(x, "\\*")) paste0(stringr::str_remove(x, "\\*$"), "\\w*") else paste0(x, "\\b")
      patterns <- purrr::map_chr(groups, \(g) paste0("\\b(", paste(purrr::map_chr(stringr::str_split_1(g, "\\|"), term), collapse = "|"), ")"))
      keep <- purrr::map(patterns, \(r) stringr::str_detect(store$text, r)) |> purrr::reduce(`&`)
      store[keep, ] |> dplyr::transmute(question, route = paste0("store-", route), key, doi, title, year, venue = container, source_note = dplyr::if_else(has_source_note == "yes", key, NA))
    }) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
  if (nrow(hits) > 0) append_csv(hits, "../02.inputs/derived/review-store-hits.csv")
  pending |>
    dplyr::transmute(strand = "library-science", route = paste0("store-", route), query = concepts, date = as.character(Sys.Date())) |>
    dplyr::mutate(retrieved = purrr::map_int(route, \(r) sum(hits$route == r)), reported_total = retrieved, cap = NA, capped = FALSE, error = NA) |>
    append_csv(search_log_path)
}
```
